source: Karger et al. (2024/25) ForecastBench
finding: Dynamic benchmark. Superforecasters beat the best LLM in 2024. Best LLMs had the market crowd forecast on market questions.
numbers: 200-item subset: superforecasters Brier 0.092, public 0.114, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.114 (p=0.001). Median superforecaster 0.091, median public 0.111. 39 superforecasters.
limits: Human vs LLM comparison on only 200 questions. Top LLMs saw the market crowd value ('freeze values').
agent_relevance: A fair baseline: the hardest rival for a model-only forecaster is a human crowd or a market price.

source: Karger et al. (2024/25) ForecastBench: no-crowd result
finding: Access to the crowd forecast mattered. LLM-crowd baseline built from 3 models x 3 superforecaster prompts.
numbers: Best model without crowd values: Brier 0.126 vs 0.114 with them. LLM crowd = 9 forecasts per question (median, geometric mean, geometric mean of log odds).
limits: Single benchmark snapshot.
agent_relevance: Reading an outside number and shrinking toward it is a cheap gain; code can do it (G5).

source: Karger et al. (2024/25) ForecastBench: combination questions
finding: LLMs do poorly on combination (conjunction) questions, widening the human gap.
numbers: With combination questions: superforecasters 0.071, public 0.090, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.124. Gap 0.053, larger than the 0.035 gap between Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Claude 2.1.
limits: Human score for combos is bounded assuming independence, which underestimates humans.
agent_relevance: Probability arithmetic across linked events should be done by code, not by the model.

source: Karger et al. (2024/25) ForecastBench: scaling trend
finding: Forecast accuracy rises with general model strength; linear extrapolation gave a parity date.
numbers: Arena score vs Brier r=-0.69 (p=0.002); parity at Arena ~1398 (95% CI 1335-1581). Log-linear in training compute R2=0.41.
limits: Extrapolation from about 17 models; CI wide.
agent_relevance: Gains so far come from the base model; do not expect a scaffold alone to close a gap.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: Retrieval + fine-tuned reasoning + ensemble nearly matches the crowd; blending with the crowd beats both.
numbers: Test 914 binary questions after June 2023. System Brier 0.179, crowd 0.149, 4:1 crowd-weighted blend 0.146, best base model no retrieval 0.208. Accuracy 71.5% vs crowd 77.0%.
limits: Beats crowd only when crowd is uncertain (0.3-0.7), early retrieval and 5+ relevant articles: 0.240 vs 0.247, covering 22% of forecasts. Calibration RMS 0.42 vs crowd 0.38.
agent_relevance: Use the model as a second opinion on uncertain cases; blend weights fixed by code.

source: Halawi et al. (2024): ablations
finding: Retrieval and fine-tuning each help; aggregation is a trimmed mean in code.
numbers: Fine-tuned GPT-3.5 0.182-0.183; base GPT-4 only 0.186; no fine-tune and no retrieval 0.206. 73,632 reasonings generated, 13,253 kept for beating the crowd. 6 forecasts per question.
limits: Fine-tuning data selected using crowd Brier.
agent_relevance: Choose by outcome-checked rationales, not by how good the reasoning reads (G2, G5).

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd
finding: An ensemble of 12 LLMs was statistically equivalent to a 925-person human crowd; averaging model and human beat letting the model see the human median.
numbers: 31 binary questions, 925 humans, 3 months. Seeing the human median improved GPT-4 and Claude 2 by 17-28%, but a plain human+machine average was better. Models predicted above 50% on average (acquiescence).
limits: Abstract page only read. Small question set, older models.
agent_relevance: Averaging independent sources beats feeding one source into another; models lean toward yes.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024/25) LLM assistants improve human forecasting
finding: Talking to an LLM advisor raised human accuracy, even a noisy advisor.
numbers: 991 analysed of 1,152. Accuracy up 24-28% vs control. Superforecasting vs noisy assistant: no difference (diff 0.04, p=.391); exploratory 41% vs 29% after dropping Q3.
limits: The superforecasting-prompt gain depended on dropping one question. No calibration results.
agent_relevance: Persona is not the driver; the benefit is a second view.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2025) Prompt engineering LLM forecasting
finding: 38 prompts on 4 models, 100 ForecastBench questions: most prompts give no reliable gain.
numbers: Mean Brier 0.208-0.227 across models. After Benjamini-Hochberg correction almost all adj p 0.77-0.99. Base-rate prompts help slightly (Base Rate First -0.016, adj p=0.036 in one model). Bayesian Reasoning prompt hurt (+0.03, p<0.001). Short superforecaster persona -0.001 (p=.93).
quote: references to base rates yield slight benefits
limits: Only 100 questions; effect sizes tiny.
agent_relevance: Do not add personas or 'think like a superforecaster'. Explicit Bayes talk degrades; keep arithmetic in code (G1, G4).

source: Schoenegger et al. (2025): o1 study
finding: Compound prompts and external prompts on o1 and o1-mini also gave no reliable gains; Bayesian Reasoning and Propose-Evaluate-Select stayed significantly worse.
numbers: Prompts still worse in more than one analysis: Bayesian Reasoning and Propose-Evaluate-Select.
limits: Small n.
agent_relevance: Test any new method prompt against a control before adopting it.

source: Wilson & Bash, Metaculus (2025) Q2 AI Benchmark
finding: Pro forecasters clearly beat the top-10 bot team in Q2 2025.
limits: Peer-score metric, not Brier; survey n=19.
agent_relevance: Multi-option questions were the weakest area.

source: Wilson & Bash, Metaculus (2025) Q2: what helped
finding: Bot-makers: base model quality dominates; aggregating several runs helps.
numbers: Survey: aggregating multiple forecasts +1,799 points (CI 1,017-2,582); testing on custom questions +2,216; manual review +1,041 (CI -223 to 2,305, n.s.). LLM calls per question r=0.40. Winner used 6-7 step research and 5 final predictions from 3 models.
limits: 19 survey responses; correlational.
agent_relevance: Several runs and mixed models, combined in code, is the supported pattern.

source: Metaculus (2026) FutureEval spring results
finding: By spring 2026 the Pro edge over the top-10 bots was no longer significant.
numbers: Head-to-head -1.25 (95% CI -4.87 to 2.37), 99 questions, p=0.247. Pros won 64% of questions. 9 of the top 10 individual places still Pros. Numeric +3.47, binary -2.51, multiple choice -5.02.
limits: Small question-type samples.
agent_relevance: The gap closed in a year; a human edge is no longer safe to assume.

source: Metaculus (2026) FutureEval: scaffold and ensembles
finding: High-reasoning bots beat standard twins; team size mattered little beyond 2.
numbers: High reasoning beat standard in 8 of 8 pairs (p=0.004). Best single-prompt baseline rank: 2nd of 96, 14th of 134, 18th of 173. Team sizes 2-10 about -2 each; top bot alone -4.51; plateau near 50.
quote: Merely increasing the size of a bot team does not automatically improve the ensemble's forecasting.
limits: Pairs not independent; survey correlations not significant after 33 tests.
agent_relevance: Bigger ensembles of the same family give little; spend compute on reasoning depth.

source: AIA Forecaster technical report (2025)
finding: Agentic search + ensemble + supervisor + Platt scaling reaches superforecaster level on ForecastBench.
numbers: FB-Market: AIA 0.0753, superforecasters 0.0740, market 0.0965, o3 0.1096. FB-7-21: AIA 0.1076 vs superforecasters 0.1110. MarketLiquid: AIA 0.1258 vs market 0.1106 (loses).
limits: Self-reported system.
agent_relevance: A code-combined loop (search, many samples, calibration). Fits S7.

source: AIA Forecaster: search ablation
finding: Agentic search beats non-agentic and no search.
numbers: No search 0.1230; non-agentic 0.1174-0.1217; agentic 0.1140-0.1182. No market price: no search 0.116, agentic search 0.085; with market price: 0.103 and 0.075; market alone 0.096.
limits: Search providers differ.
agent_relevance: Retrieval carries most of the gain; it is real outside output (G2).

source: AIA Forecaster: calibration and aggregation in code
finding: Statistical post-hoc fixes beat model-based fixes. Platt scaling best; LLM supervisor and best-of-k worse.
numbers: FB-7-21: none 0.1140; Platt (sqrt3) 0.1076; log-odds extremization 0.1085; isotonic 0.1097; OLS 0.1119. Mean of 10 forecasts 0.1140 vs single 0.1182. Agentic supervisor 0.1125, best-of-k 0.1191.
limits: Fixed coefficient sqrt3 chosen by authors. Conflicts with G4 only if extremizing is blind; here it is calibrated on data.
agent_relevance: Direct Meehl pattern: code does the final combination. Fit any scaling on held-out data.

source: AIA Forecaster: blend with market
finding: Combining model and market helps only where the model is weaker.
numbers: MarketLiquid: weights 0.33 AIA / 0.67 market, Brier 0.126 / 0.111 / ensemble 0.106. FB-Market: 0.87/0.14, ensemble 0.079 worse than AIA 0.075. About 1.65% of search results had foreknowledge.
limits: Leave-one-out weights.
agent_relevance: Weight blends by measured track record, in code.

source: Lu et al. (2025) Outcome-based RL to predict the future
finding: A 14B model trained with outcome rewards matches o1 on forecasting.
numbers: 1,265 test questions. Base 0.215; trained ensemble 0.190; o1 0.202; Polymarket 0.151. ROI about 10%; about 20% for market prices 40-60%. Without guardrails 39.3% of predictions fell in 0-10% or 90-100%.
limits: The market itself beat every model; trading simulation is simplified.
agent_relevance: Training only; shows drift to overconfidence without limits.

source: Paleka et al. (2024) Consistency checks for LLM forecasters
finding: Logical consistency of forecasts tracks accuracy and can be measured at once.
numbers: Correlation with Brier (arbitrage metric): Cond 0.92 scraped, 0.71 NewsAPI; Negation 0.60 vs -0.36 on NewsAPI. o1-mini Cond violation 41% / 66%, Negation 58% / 52%.
limits: Confounded by model strength. ArbitrageForecaster did not generalise to held-out checks or improve Brier.
agent_relevance: Code-run coherence checks (G5) are a cheap signal when no truth is available.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Pitfalls in evaluating LLM forecasters
finding: Names temporal leakage and poor extrapolation to real forecasting as the two evaluation problems.
numbers: Search result summary only.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Treat retrospective numbers cautiously.

source: El Lahib et al. (2026) Temporal leakage in date-filtered search
finding: Date filters in search leak the future; retrospective Brier looks far better than real.
numbers: gpt-oss-120b, 93 binary questions: leaky docs Brier 0.108, leak-free 0.242, no retrieval 0.244. 33.2% of Google and 34.5% of DuckDuckGo URLs leaky; 71.0% / 81.2% of 393 / 389 questions had a major leak.
limits: Mitigation only suggested, not tested.
agent_relevance: Our own tests with retrieval must use frozen snapshots (G3).

source: Simulated Ignorance Fails (2026)
finding: Telling a model to forget post-cutoff events does not work.
numbers: 9 models, 477 (or 470) questions. Pre-cutoff Brier 0.11 vs post-cutoff 0.24; instructions close only 48% of the 52% gap. Humans 0.232 vs 0.243.
limits: Question count mismatch inside paper.
agent_relevance: Do not evaluate with prompted ignorance.

source: Hegselmann et al. (2022) TabLLM
finding: Serialised tables let LLMs classify; competitive with gradient boosting in very-few-shot.
numbers: Abstract: zero-shot 'non-trivial'; best in very-few-shot.
limits: Abstract only read.
agent_relevance: LLM is a weak substitute for fitted models once data exist.

source: Zero-training LLMs on small tabular data (2025)
finding: LLMs are fair at small classification, bad at regression.
numbers: Lupus (87 rows): logistic regression 0.8889; GPT-4o 0.8333; GPT-5 0.7778; Gemini 0.6667. Bankrupt: LR 1.0, GPT-5 1.0. Diabetes R2: linear 0.4526, GPT-o3 -1.41. Servo R2: CatBoost 0.95, GPT-5t 0.89, GPT-o3 -0.005.
limits: Tiny samples; paper has table errors (Friedman rows copied).
agent_relevance: When data fit a regression, let code fit it; the model reads features only.

source: Malin et al. (2025) LLMs less effective than local ML for clinical prediction
finding: Zero-shot GPT-3.5/4 lose clearly to trained ML in EHR prediction.
numbers: AUROC VUMC/MIMIC: ML 0.847/0.894; GPT-4 0.629/0.602; GPT-3.5 0.537/0.517. Brier VUMC: ML 0.134, GPT-3.5 0.384, GPT-4 0.251. In-context examples did not close the gap.
limits: Non-fine-tuned 2023-24 models. Read via Europe PMC full text.
agent_relevance: Clinical-vs-statistical pattern repeated in LLMs: holistic LLM judgment loses to a fitted combination.

source: TEMED-LLM (2023) LLM extracts features, models classify
finding: Model fills a feature table, a fitted model combines it: beats direct LLM classification and text classifiers.
numbers: Heart: xgboost 0.985 accuracy vs direct text-davinci-003 10-shot 0.620; logreg 0.860. Hepatitis xgboost 0.992 vs 0.642; Stroke 0.740 vs 0.558. Extraction accuracy 0.92-0.99.
limits: Small sets (110-917 records); inconsistent feature counts in the paper.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to S7: model scores features, code combines.

source: ClinStructor (2025) structured extraction from clinical text
finding: Search summary: structured question-answer features cost about 2-3% AUC vs direct fine-tuning but add transparency.
numbers: About -2 to -3% AUC.
limits: Search result only, not opened.
agent_relevance: Structure is not free in accuracy; its value is auditability.

source: LoID (2026) LLM logits as Bayesian priors
finding: Reading LLM next-token probabilities as priors for logistic regression helps under covariate shift.
numbers: 10 tabular datasets. Closes up to 59% of gap to full-data oracle. Beats AutoElicit on 8/10 (loses Heart 0.90 vs 0.92). Bank Marketing 0.72 vs OOD-LR 0.51 vs oracle 0.89. Wrong-sign priors 0-6% vs 20-50% for sampled elicitation.
limits: Gemma-2-27B; synthetic shifts.
agent_relevance: Model supplies priors, regression fits weights: a Meehl-style division of labour.

source: Recht (2025) The Actuary's Final Word on Algorithmic Decision Making
finding: Reviews Meehl, Grove 2000 and Aegisdottir 2006; says statistical rules win when outcomes are few and data machine-readable; LLMs widen 'machine-readable'.
numbers: Grove et al.: 136 predictions, mechanical clearly better (>=0.05) in 46%, comparable in 48%, clinical clearly better in <6%. Aegisdottir: 48 predictions, 52% statistical, 38% comparable, 10% clinical.
limits: Secondary account of earlier meta-analyses; argument paper.
agent_relevance: Boundary: Meehl's win needs a small outcome set and recorded inputs; open-ended tasks differ.

source: Fragile Families Challenge (Salganik et al. 2020, via search)
finding: 160 teams with machine learning barely beat a 4-variable regression.
numbers: Best submissions only slightly better than benchmark regression with four expert-chosen predictors.
limits: Search summary only; no LLMs.
agent_relevance: Boundary: where outcomes are intrinsically uncertain, no combiner helps much.

source: LifeSentence (2026) language model on life-event sequences
finding: A language model trained on event sequences beats logistic regression and XGBoost for next life event.
numbers: N=65,606 (52,485 train). Event accuracy 61.6% vs LR 52.9%, XGBoost 58.2%, LSTM 56.4%. Joint accuracy 35.3% vs 8.6% and 15.0%.
limits: Trained model, not prompted; rich data.
agent_relevance: Boundary: richer learned models can beat linear ones.

source: Forecasting Research Institute (2026) parity post
finding: By July 2026 several AI systems are statistically indistinguishable from superforecasters on ForecastBench.
numbers: One-sided p against equal accuracy: Cassi AI 0.41, xAI 0.16/0.15, DeepMind 0.14. 17 submissions above superforecasters on preliminary dataset questions. A system ranked above the superforecaster median on market questions.
limits: Superforecaster data from 2024; CIs overlap.
agent_relevance: Human-expert edge is gone; test against a calibrated market baseline.
